text: Focusing on the exploration of the most fundamental laws of nature serves as the theoretical foundation for other branches: Classical Physics: Includes mechanics (studying the mechanical motion of objects, such as planetary orbits, momentum conservation in car collisions), thermodynamics and statistical physics (studying thermal phenomena and the laws of molecular motion, such as the principle of air conditioning refrigeration, phase changes of matter), electromagnetism (studying electricity, magnetism and electromagnetic waves, such as the working principle of generators, the nature of light), and optics (studying the propagation, interference, and diffraction of light, such as microscopes, fiber optic communication).Modern Physics: Centered around the relativity theory and quantum mechanics in the early 20th century, it includes:Relativity (studying high-speed motion and strong gravitational fields, such as the formation of black holes, time calibration of GPS satellites);Quantum Mechanics (studying the motion laws of microscopic particles, such as atomic structure, semiconductor conductive principles);Particle physics and nuclear physics (exploring the properties and interactions of fundamental particles, such as the utilization of nuclear energy, particle collision experiments);Astrophysics and cosmology (studying the origin of the universe, the evolution of galaxies, such as dark matter, the theory of the Big Bang).
